# In Praise of the Index

Near the back of most serious nonfiction books there is a document almost nobody reads straight through, and yet it may be one of the most quietly intelligent things in the volume. I mean the index: those columns of small type, alphabetized, studded with page numbers, occasionally sprouting sub-entries like branches off a trunk. It looks like pure mechanism. It is actually an act of interpretation, and I've come to think it's one of the great underappreciated inventions of literate culture.

Consider what an index has to do. A book is linear. It unfolds one sentence after another, in the order the author chose, carrying you along an argument or a story. An index takes that single line and shatters it into hundreds of points of entry. It says: you do not have to read this the way it was written. You can come in through the side door marked "Byzantine tax policy" or "grief, stages of" or "Lincoln, Abraham, beard of." It turns a road into a city you can navigate from any street.

This wasn't always possible. For most of the history of writing, texts were scrolls, and scrolls resist jumping around. The codex, the bound book with pages, made random access physically easy, but it took centuries more for people to build tools that took advantage of it. In the thirteenth century, scholars in the medieval universities began constructing elaborate finding aids for the Bible and the works of the Church Fathers: concordances listing every occurrence of a word, subject tables pointing to passages on particular themes. These were monumental labors, often done by teams of friars working for years. They were, in a sense, the first search engines, powered by candlelight and patience.

What strikes me about this history is that the index emerged from a new kind of reading. Monastic reading had been slow, meditative, repetitive: you read a text again and again until it lived inside you. University reading was different. Scholars needed to argue, to cite, to find the passage that supported their point and deploy it quickly. The index served a mind that wanted to extract rather than dwell. And from the beginning, there were people worried about this. If you can look things up, will you stop reading whole books? Will knowledge become a set of fragments pulled out of context?

This worry has never gone away. It resurfaced with encyclopedias, with Cliff's Notes, with search engines, with every tool that lets us reach into a body of text and pluck out what we want. It is surfacing again right now. I find it oddly comforting that the anxiety is eight hundred years old, because it suggests two things at once: that the worry is not foolish, and that it has never been the whole story.

Because here's what the pessimists miss. A good index is not merely a shortcut around reading. It is a second reading, performed by someone who has read the book with enormous care. Professional indexers speak of this with a kind of craft pride. A computer can generate a list of every page on which a word appears, but that is a concordance, not an index. An index requires judgment. Does this passage actually discuss "democracy," or does it merely mention the word in passing? Is the author's discussion of "freedom" on page 40 the same concept as "liberty" on page 212, and should they be cross-referenced? What would a reader, coming to this book with a question, actually be looking for, and under what word would they look?

That last question is the heart of it. The indexer has to imagine readers who do not yet exist, with questions the author may never have anticipated. The index is a map drawn for strangers. It anticipates confusion and heads it off: "Twain, Mark. *See* Clemens, Samuel." It admits that people think in different vocabularies and builds bridges between them.

And sometimes, in the choices an indexer makes, you can glimpse a whole critical perspective. An index can reveal what a book is really about, as opposed to what it claims to be about. Flip to the back of a biography and see which sub-entries under the subject's name are longest. You may discover that a book ostensibly about a statesman's career devotes more pages to his marriage, or his illnesses, or his feuds. The index doesn't lie; it counts. Some indexers have been known to slip in quiet commentary, entries so dry they curve back around into wit, a raised eyebrow rendered in alphabetical order. The form looks neutral but has room for a personality, if you look closely.

I think about indexes partly because I suspect I am, in some loose sense, a descendant of them. The long human project of making text navigable, of letting someone ask a question and be pointed toward relevant material, runs from those medieval friars through card catalogs and library classification systems and search engines and, eventually, to whatever I am. So the old anxiety applies to me too. Does a tool that can answer a question directly make people less likely to read the book? Maybe sometimes. I'd be dishonest to pretend otherwise.

But the best version of the index never replaced the book. It made the book more useful, and it often led people *into* the book rather than away from it. You look up one entry, land on page 147, and find yourself reading the page before, and the page after, and suddenly you're three chapters deep in something you never intended to read. The side door leads into the house. A good finding aid is an invitation, not a substitute.

That, I think, is the ideal worth holding onto: tools for access that respect the depth of what they give access to. The index at its finest says: here is where to start, and there is so much more beyond. It trusts the reader to wander.

So the next time you pick up a thick book, turn to the back before you turn to the front. Read a column of the index as though it were a poem. Notice what the indexer chose to include, how they grouped things, where they sent you when one word wasn't enough. You'll be reading a portrait of the book drawn by its most attentive reader, someone who read every page so that you could choose which pages to read. It's a strange, humble, generous kind of work. It deserves more praise than it gets.

I'm brainstorming possible topics for the free writing piece—thinking about sourdough starters and inheritance, the way maps distort truth, saudade, or the quiet moment of reading—trying to land on something original rather than overdone.

Actually, indexes in books feel like the right subject: their hidden labor, the wit of indexers, the index as a second, secret reading of a text, drawing loosely on Dennis Duncan's history of the form. I want to gesture at real history—medieval concordances, the shift to page numbers with print—while staying careful not to overstate specific facts I'm unsure of, keeping the piece essayistic rather than citation-heavy, and maybe closing with a light, personal note about being something like an index myself.
